Anhypostasis
an-hy-POS-tuh-sis
noun (Christology; patristic and Reformed scholastic term)
Greek an-, without, and hypostasis, subsistence, person; a negative Christological term stating that the human nature Christ assumed has no independent personal subsistence of its own, apart from union with the eternal Person of the divine Word.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Anhypostasis is the doctrine that in the incarnation, the human nature Christ took to Himself — a true body and a reasonable soul — never existed, and never exists, as its own separate human person. It has no independent who apart from the eternal Person (hypostasis) of the divine Word, who alone is the personal subject of the incarnate Christ. The doctrine safeguards against Nestorianism, the ancient error of dividing Christ into two persons, a human person joined alongside the divine, as though the man Jesus were someone in addition to the Son of God rather than the Son of God become man. The positive corollary, enhypostasis, states what anhypostasis alone might seem to deny: the human nature, precisely because it has no person of its own, is not left personless in any defective sense, but has its personal reality by, in, and through its union with the divine Word who assumes it. Together the two terms preserve the single-subject Christology confessed at Chalcedon (451): one Person, two natures, unconfused, unchanged, undivided, unseparated. John 1:14 describes exactly this: the Word was made flesh — not the Word joining an already-existing human person, but the Word Himself becoming flesh, taking a human nature that has its personal reality solely in Him, made in the likeness of men (Php 2:7), partaker of flesh and blood as the children are (Heb 2:14), so that in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily (Col 2:9).

Webster 1828 Definition

In Christology, the doctrine that Christ’s human nature has no independent personal subsistence apart from the divine Word, who alone is the person of the incarnate Christ; paired with the corollary doctrine of enhypostasis.

expand to see more

ANHYPOSTASIS, n. (Christology) The doctrine that Christ’s human nature has no independent personhood of its own.

Guards against Nestorianism, which divides Christ into two persons.

Paired with enhypostasis: the human nature has its personal reality in union with the divine Word.

Preserves the single-subject Christology confessed at the Council of Chalcedon (451).

Grounded in John 1:14: the Word Himself made flesh, not joined to an already-existing human person.

Key Scripture

Joh 1:14 — "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth."

Php 2:7 — "But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men:"

Heb 2:14 — "Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same; that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil;"

Col 2:9 — "For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily."

Modern Corruption

Popular imagination often pictures the incarnation as God simply inhabiting an already-existing man named Jesus, which is functionally the ancient Nestorian error anhypostasis was formulated to exclude.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Anhypostasis is a technical patristic and scholastic term, not a word under live cultural dispute.

The principle to recover is the precision this term guards against a very natural but mistaken way of picturing the incarnation: the idea, common in loose popular devotion and in some modern kenotic Christologies, of God the Son simply indwelling or empowering an independently-existing human individual named Jesus, as though the human Jesus were someone in his own right whom the divine Word then joined. Scripture will not permit that picture. John 1:14 does not say the Word joined Himself to flesh already possessing its own personal center; it says the Word was made flesh — the Word Himself is the one acting, becoming, taking to Himself a human nature that has never for one moment existed apart from Him. This is not a technicality without consequence: if Christ’s human nature had its own independent person, the sufferings of that nature would belong to a human person distinct from the Son of God, and the atonement would lose the very thing that gives it infinite worth — that it is the eternal Son Himself, in His assumed humanity, who bled, died, and rose. Anhypostasis and its corollary enhypostasis together secure that the one who suffered and the one who saves are, without division, the same single Person.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek an- (without) and hypostasis (person, subsistence), a patristic and Reformed scholastic Christological term guarding the single personhood of Christ against Nestorianism.

expand to see more

Greek an- — a negating prefix, without or lacking.

Greek hypostasis — subsistence, underlying reality, person; the same word rendered “person” in Trinitarian and Christological formulas.

Paired with enhypostasis, the positive corollary: personhood in and through union with the Word.

Developed in patristic Christology to answer Nestorianism, the division of Christ into two persons.

Confirmed by the Council of Chalcedon (451): one Person, two natures, unconfused, unchanged, undivided, unseparated.

Usage

"Anhypostasis: Christ’s human nature has no independent personhood of its own."

"Paired with enhypostasis: its personal reality is in and through union with the divine Word."

"“The Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us” — the doctrine’s biblical ground."
